one_liner: Book sample: one scalar saxpy loop compiled per ISA (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512F) with CPUID dispatch; 1.27-1.35x over default build.
what_it_does: A chapter-4 sample from a Packt C++ book showing hand-rolled function multiversioning: CMake's configure_file stamps one plain loop (y[i] += a*x[i] over std::span) into saxpy_default, saxpy_sse42, saxpy_avx2 and saxpy_avx512f, each source compiled with its own -m flag (/arch: on MSVC), and ct::saxpy picks one at run time from CPUID feature bits. A hand-written AVX2 intrinsics version (saxpy_hand) and OpenBLAS cblas_saxpy are benchmarked alongside. The benchmark calls each variant directly on 5,120 floats; the ct::saxpy dispatcher itself is never timed.
how_it_is_fast: No new algorithm: the compiler auto-vectorises the same loop at a wider width when allowed a newer instruction set (4 floats per SSE register, 8 per AVX2, 16 per AVX-512), and run-time CPUID dispatch lets one binary use the widest copy the CPU supports while still running on baseline x86-64. The book's gains (1.27x for AVX2, 1.35x for AVX-512F over the SSE2 default) are far below the width ratios, consistent with SAXPY doing two loads and one store per multiply-add, so cache bandwidth rather than arithmetic sets the pace; the two 20 KB arrays (40 KB together) exceed a 32 KB L1 data cache (derived). SSE4.2 adds no float arithmetic over SSE2 for this loop, which matches its unchanged time.
when_to_use: Shipping one x86-64 binary to a mixed fleet where a hot, simple, auto-vectorisable loop should use AVX2 or AVX-512 when present without raising the baseline ISA.
When you want explicit control over which ISA tiers are built and how they are chosen, rather than GCC/Clang's [[gnu::target_clones]] (which the same repository uses in Chapter-14/saxpy_mt.cpp).
Element-wise kernels with more arithmetic per byte than SAXPY, where wider vectors should pay off more than the 1.3x seen here (general expectation, not measured in the repository).
Learning how per-ISA builds, CPUID feature bits and dispatch fit together before adopting target_clones or a SIMD library.
when_not_to_use: Calling ct::saxpy on small arrays in a hot path as written: the dispatcher calls get_best_instructions(), two or three CPUID instructions, on every call with no caching; CPUID is serialising and under virtualisation it normally traps to the hypervisor, which can rival the roughly 300 ns of work at N = 5,120 (derived; the dispatcher is never timed).
Large, memory-resident arrays: SAXPY is bandwidth-bound, so wider vectors gain little once the data leave cache; only one cache-resident size (5,120 floats) is benchmarked.

Non-x86 targets, MSVC or 32-bit builds: my_cpuid.h expands to static_assert(false) on non-x86 targets, tests __MSVC__ (MSVC defines _MSC_VER) so cl.exe gets no my_cpuid definition, and tests __X86__ rather than __i386__ so 32-bit GCC also hits the static_assert.
Machines or VMs whose OS has not enabled AVX or AVX-512 register state: get_best_instructions() reads CPUID feature bits only, without the OSXSAVE/XGETBV check, so it can select a copy that faults.
When you want BLAS-grade performance across sizes: the auto-vectorised copies edge out OpenBLAS only at this one small size, where call overhead weighs most.

integration.form: source-drop (saxpy.cpp.in template, saxpy.h, the saxpy.cpp dispatcher, get_best_instructions.h, my_cpuid.h and the CMake configure_file loop that adds per-file -m flags)
integration.dependencies: none for the kernels; the benchmark needs Google Benchmark and optionally a BLAS with cblas.h (CMake asks for a static ILP64 BLAS via BLA_SIZEOF_INTEGER 8 and BLA_STATIC ON and silently drops the OpenBLAS row if none is found); the shared Chapter-04 project also requires GTest, Threads and OpenMP at configure time
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (std::span), CMake 3.30+, GCC or Clang targeting x86-64 (<cpuid.h>, -msse4.2/-mavx2/-mavx512f)
integration.platforms: x86-64 only, with GCC or Clang (clang-cl defines __clang__ and should work); plain MSVC cl.exe and 32-bit GCC do not compile my_cpuid.h as written; the AVX-512F tier needs an AVX-512F CPU
integration.thread_safety: The kernels are stateless and safe on disjoint output spans; the dispatcher keeps no state (it re-queries CPUID on every call), so it is thread-safe but slow.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: ct::saxpy has the same signature as saxpy_default and computes the same mul-then-add, but it needs the per-ISA CMake setup, and its per-call CPUID should be cached before it is worth calling on small arrays.

gotchas: Cache the dispatch: store the get_best_instructions() result once (a function-local static or a function pointer) or use target_clones/ifunc as Chapter-14 does; as shipped, every ct::saxpy call pays several CPUID instructions.

-mavx2 does not imply -mfma, so the avx2 tier and saxpy_hand issue a separate multiply and add; -mavx2 -mfma (or -march=x86-64-v3) is the fairer AVX2 tier, and any tier that fuses the multiply-add can differ from the default build in the last bit.
Neither the per-ISA loops nor saxpy_hand check that x is at least as long as y; only the dispatcher asserts it, and assert compiles away under NDEBUG, so a short x is read out of bounds.

Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a plain configure builds without optimisation and none of the tiers vectorise; configure Release. Per-file -mavx2/-mavx512f flags also risk the linker keeping an AVX-compiled copy of an inline header function for the default path (a general hazard of per-file ISA flags, not observed in this repo). Open PR #14 (unmerged) fixes build errors in the chapter's gemm files, so build the bench_saxpy target alone if the full project fails.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this pattern when a few simple loops already auto-vectorise and you only need ISA selection; xsimd or Vc give explicit SIMD types at the cost of rewriting the kernel, NumKong ships ready-made dispatched dot-product and distance kernels, and SLEEF or fmath cover transcendental functions that per-ISA recompilation alone does not speed up.
verified_claims_summary: The repository holds code only; the book's run, relayed by the seed lead, times the same scalar loop on 5,120 floats at 329 ns (default x86-64 build), 330 ns (SSE4.2), 259 ns (AVX2), 243 ns (AVX-512F) and 298 ns for hand-written AVX2 intrinsics, against 278 ns for OpenBLAS cblas_saxpy, so the AVX-512F and AVX2 builds are about 1.35x and 1.27x faster than the default build and the hand intrinsics lose to the compiler. Compiler, optimisation level, OpenBLAS version and the AVX-512-capable CPU are not stated, and the CPUID dispatcher a real caller goes through is not timed.
status_note: Packt book companion repository, MIT-licensed, 20 stars and 8 forks; the last commit (2026-01-22) changed only the README and the code last changed in November 2025, with one open issue (#15, about the clamp loop) and one unmerged build-fix PR (#14); the pattern is a handful of small files to copy, but fix the per-call CPUID and the compiler-macro checks first.
